name: Homes
protects: Sleep, care work, and the older people, young children and sick people who spend the hottest hours indoors.

kitchen.title: Kitchen heat
kitchen.brief: Cooking adds heat on top of the weather, often in the smallest room and usually for women; in Nepal’s Madhesh Province it falls hardest on women in the poorest single-room homes.
kitchen.text: Cooking adds heat on top of the weather, often in the smallest, least ventilated room, and usually for women. In Nepal’s Madhesh Province, women cooking in hot, smoky kitchens carry a daily ‘thermal labour’ that falls hardest on women in the poorest single-room homes with little access to clean energy or credit.
questions: How much heat does the stove give off, and does anyone sit beside it for long?
Can hot air and smoke get out: a window, a vent, a gap under the roof?
Is there smoke from wood, dung or kerosene adding to the strain?
How long is cooking each day, and can some of it move to cooler hours?
Can the household afford cleaner fuel through the season, not only once?
Is the electricity reliable enough for a fan or an electric cooker when it is hottest?

source.label: Ghimire and others, Frontiers in Public Health, 2025

caution: Check the roof type, fire safety, tenure and ventilation before any retrofit.
measure: Indoor temperature at 3 p.m. in treated and untreated homes, logged through the season

options.name: Reflective roof coating
options.does: A white, solar-reflective coat on the roof, so less of the sun’s heat passes into the room below.
options.keeps: Repainting every few years, and a thermometer to check it works.
options.avoid: Promising a fixed number of degrees before you have measured.

src.label: Telangana Cool Roof Policy coverage, 2023: about ₹300 per m²

options.name: Lime whitewash
options.does: A cheap seasonal white coat that households can apply themselves when a commercial coating is out of reach.
options.keeps: Recoating every season, by a named group.
options.avoid: Treating it as a lasting retrofit.

options.name: Better roof panels
options.does: Replace or cover thin tin or asbestos sheets with an insulated roof panel.
options.keeps: A structural check, and secure enough tenure to make the investment safe.
options.avoid: Scaling up before checking structure and tenure.

options.name: Insulation under the roof
options.does: A fire-safe layer or false ceiling that slows heat coming through the roof.
options.keeps: A fire-safety review of the material.
options.avoid: Flammable sheets near kitchens or wiring.

options.name: Shade on walls and windows
options.does: Bamboo blinds, jute screens or awnings on the sunny side stop sunlight before it reaches the room.
options.keeps: Fixing and replacing screens each season.
options.avoid: Blocking airflow or all daylight.

options.name: Let the air through
options.does: Higher vents and openings that let hot air out at night.
options.keeps: Security, rain protection and mosquito screens.
options.avoid: Openings that let in dust, rain or intruders.

facts.fact: In 16 homes in an Ahmedabad informal settlement, measured in September 2017, rooms under a modular roof averaged about 33.8 °C against 36.8 °C under asbestos sheets. White paint on tin did not beat asbestos or concrete in the same comparison: measure before you promise.

source.label: Vellingiri et al., Indian Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine, 2020

facts.fact: In a two-year trial in Burkina Faso, cool roofs lowered indoor temperatures by 1.2 °C in tin-and-mud homes and 1.7 °C in tin-roofed homes, and residents’ heart rates fell. The same team began a year-long trial in about 400 Ahmedabad homes in 2025.

source.label: Reuters, via South China Morning Post, 2025

name: Outdoor work
protects: People whose income depends on being outdoors in the hottest hours: vendors, loaders, builders, sanitation workers, traffic police.
caution: A shelter without water, paid rest or a change of hours is not worker protection.
measure: Workers within a few minutes’ walk of shade and water, and rest breaks actually taken

options.name: Rest shelters on work routes
options.does: Shade, seating and water where workers can recover during a shift.
options.keeps: Paid rest time, and someone who cleans and refills it.
options.avoid: Treating the shelter as a substitute for work rules.

options.name: Drinking water and rehydration salts
options.does: Refill points with safe water and oral rehydration salts at markets, sites and junctions.
options.keeps: A daily refill and cleaning roster, often ₹500–2,000 a day.
options.avoid: Counting it as cooling: it protects bodies, not temperatures.

options.name: Shade nets
options.does: Quick shade over junctions, queues and work yards.
options.keeps: Poles set firmly into the ground, and nets up before the heat starts.
options.avoid: Bamboo frames that fall in the first storm.

options.name: Shade trees on work routes
options.does: Canopy along the streets where people work and wait.
options.keeps: Water, root space and three years of care.
options.avoid: Counting saplings planted instead of canopy that survives.

options.name: Misting at hotspots
options.does: Fine water spray at a few crowded, dry spots.
options.keeps: Safe water, drainage, filters and a technician.
options.avoid: Humid places and water-short cities: in humid heat the benefit roughly halves.

facts.fact: Nagpur strung green shade nets over 10–12 busy junctions in May 2026. Several tore or collapsed in strong winds, and residents pointed out the heat had begun at the end of March. A net had also fallen at Tukdoji Square in 2025 because its bamboo was not set firmly into the road.
Comparing Phoenix with humid Houston, misters still cut heat stress in the humid city, but with about half the benefit, and only when there was some wind.

source.label: US National Science Foundation public access repository

name: Schools and childcare
protects: Learning, play, attendance and drinking water for children and the staff who look after them.
caution: Count shade and surviving trees, not saplings planted.
measure: Classroom temperature at 2 p.m. before and after, and school days lost to heat

options.name: Cool classroom roofs
options.does: A reflective coat or a ventilated second roof over the hottest classrooms.
options.keeps: A line in the school’s maintenance budget.
options.avoid: Roof canopies that are not anchored for monsoon winds.

options.name: Shaded play space
options.does: Trees, shade structures and less hard paving where children play.
options.keeps: Watering through the holidays, when nobody is at school.
options.avoid: Planting that dies in the first summer break.

cost.unit: school, from basic greening to a full package

options.name: Shade on classroom windows
options.does: Screens or awnings on the sunny side of classrooms.
options.keeps: Fixing them back after each monsoon.
options.avoid: Making rooms so dark that lights and fans run all day.

options.name: Drinking water at school
options.does: Enough safe, cool water for every child, with time in the timetable to drink it.
options.keeps: Filter changes and cleaning.
options.avoid: One tap for hundreds of children.

facts.fact: Researchers who studied how age groups use green spaces found that older people asked for benches, shelter during extreme weather and safe paths, while children wanted trees for shade and places to play. Ask both before you design.

source.label: Frantzeskaki et al., chapter 11 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023

name: Markets and street vending
protects: Vendors’ income and stock, customers, and the porters who load and unload in the heat.
caution: Design it with the vendors and protect their place, or the upgrade becomes an eviction.
measure: Vendors with shade and water at their stall, and vendors still trading there a year later

options.name: Shade over stalls and aisles
options.does: Nets, fabric or a light frame with climbing plants over the places vendors sit.
options.keeps: Storm-proof fixing and someone to replace worn cloth.
options.avoid: Shade that blocks fire access or loading.

options.name: Water and rehydration points
options.does: Safe drinking water for vendors and customers.
options.keeps: A refill and cleaning roster agreed with the market association.
options.avoid: Points nobody is responsible for.

options.name: Planted drains and rain gardens
options.does: Planted channels and hollows that soak up runoff so the market does not flood after a storm.
options.keeps: Rubbish collection, or they clog.
options.avoid: Building them where waste is dumped.

options.name: A whole-market package
options.does: Shade, water, cool roofs, drainage, trees and waste collection together, run with the vendors.
options.keeps: A vendor committee with a say over the design and the upkeep.
options.avoid: Beautification that pushes informal vendors out.

facts.fact: India’s Street Vendors Act (2014) gives vendors 40% of the seats on each town vending committee and says no vendor may be evicted or relocated until a survey of existing vendors is complete: a hook for designing market cooling with vendors, not around them.

source.label: Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act, 2014, on FAOLEX

name: Bus stops and queues
protects: Commuters, patients queuing at clinics, people waiting for rations or wages, and visitors.
caution: Put the shade where people actually stand, at the hours they wait.
measure: People waiting in shade at the busiest hour, counted at each stop

options.name: Cool waiting points
options.does: Shade, a bench, drinking water and a board showing the heat alert, at bus stops, clinics and ration shops.
options.keeps: Access for older and disabled people, and someone who refills the water.
options.avoid: Counting shelters built instead of people protected.

options.name: Planted bus stops
options.does: Climbers on a frame that shade the stop more each year.
options.keeps: Watering and pruning.
options.avoid: Living shade with no water plan.

options.name: Trees where queues form
options.does: Canopy over the places people wait every day.
options.keeps: Root space, water and three years of care.
options.avoid: Planting where the queue isn’t.

options.name: Shorter waits
options.does: Appointment slots, token systems and timed services so fewer people stand in the sun at midday.
options.keeps: Agreement from the clinic, office or transport operator.
options.avoid: Assuming shade is the only answer.

facts.fact: Measuring how hot people actually feel on summer days in Tempe, Arizona, researchers found shade from buildings cooled most by day, then trees, then light structures such as sails. Air temperature barely differed between them, and every kind of shade held heat after sunset.

source.label: Middel et al., 50 Grades of Shade, Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society

name: Heat and waterlogging
protects: Neighbourhoods that bake in summer and flood in the monsoon, and the groundwater both depend on.
caution: Stop sewage and rubbish flowing in, and fund the desilting, before calling it blue-green.
measure: Waterlogging hours after heavy rain, and summer temperature near the site, before and after

options.name: Sponge parks
options.does: Small parks shaped to hold, soak up and slowly release stormwater, with plants that cool the area around them.
options.keeps: An overflow, mosquito control and desilting before each monsoon.
options.avoid: Standing water.

src.label: Chennai: 57 sponge parks commissioned for ₹7.67 crore, about ₹13.5 lakh each by our arithmetic

options.name: Restored ponds and lakes
options.does: Desilted, protected water bodies with planted edges that store floodwater, recharge groundwater and cool their surroundings.
options.keeps: Sewage diverted away, and rubbish kept out.
options.avoid: Calling a polluted pond a cooling asset.

src.label: Chennai: one pond restored for ₹36 lakh

options.name: Planted drains and rain gardens
options.does: Channels and hollows that slow, clean and soak up runoff from roofs and lanes.
options.keeps: Rubbish collection and an overflow.
options.avoid: Places where they will become open garbage drains.

options.name: Permeable paving
options.does: Paving that lets rain soak in instead of running off.
options.keeps: Regular cleaning so it does not clog.
options.avoid: Claiming it cools unless there is shade and moist soil too.

options.name: Recharge pits
options.does: Small pits that send roof and courtyard runoff into the ground.
options.keeps: A filter, so polluted water does not reach shallow wells.
options.avoid: Recharging dirty runoff.

facts.fact: Over four years, Greater Chennai Corporation restored 70 ponds for ₹144.34 crore and built 88 rainwater-harvesting parks for ₹14.74 crore.
Bangkok’s Benjakitti Forest Park, a former tobacco factory turned wetland, is designed to hold 87 million litres of water.

China’s sponge-city pilots in 30 cities (2014–2019) often built projects one at a time instead of as a city-wide system, struggled to get engineers and designers working together, and left cities worried about paying for more once pilot money ended.

source.label: McPhillips et al., chapter 7 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023

facts.fact: Jakarta’s green space was about 5.2–5.6% of the city in 2024–25, sources differ, against a legal target of 30%, now pushed back to 2045.

name: Greening where water is short
protects: Trees, soil moisture and groundwater, and the long-term shade they give.
caution: Planting without water, soil care and a survival budget is not adaptation.
measure: Trees alive and growing after three years, against trees planted

options.name: Care for the trees you have
options.does: Better tree pits, mulch, compost and looser soil so existing trees take up water and survive.
options.keeps: A yearly care round.
options.avoid: Replanting instead of fixing why trees die.

options.name: Rainwater for trees
options.does: Store runoff from roofs and streets to water trees and gardens through dry spells.
options.keeps: Clean tanks and a plan for the dry months.
options.avoid: Planting with no water source at all.

options.name: Treated wastewater for parks
options.does: Use treated water from a treatment plant for parks and tree corridors, so greenery does not compete with drinking water.
options.keeps: Treatment that is checked.
options.avoid: Untreated sewage on public land.

options.name: Street trees with three years’ care
options.does: Hardy, shade-giving species, chosen for the heat and drought ahead.
options.keeps: Species choice, root space, water and a named owner.
options.avoid: Counting planted trees.

options.name: Dense mini-forests
options.does: Small, densely planted native woods on spare public land.
options.keeps: Water through the first years.
options.avoid: Assuming they beat ordinary shade trees on value.

facts.fact: In Berlin’s Johannisthal park, more than 500 of 870 newly planted native trees died within ten years despite watering, so the shade and cooling never arrived. Across the city, about 44,000 street trees were cut between 2012 and 2019 and about 18,000 planted.

source.label: Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023

facts.fact: In Santiago de Chile, how well a municipality manages its trees was the strongest predictor of whether they survive, and wealthier municipalities spend far more on it.

source.label: Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023

name: Making it last
protects: Every asset above: who targets it, who opens it on an alert, who pays for upkeep, and who hears complaints.
caution: Often the most useful layer, and the easiest to leave unfunded.
measure: Cooling assets still working after three years, each with a named owner and an upkeep budget

options.name: Link the heat plan to the assets
options.does: A ward or settlement plan that says which shelters, water points and cool spaces open at each alert level, and who opens them.
options.keeps: A yearly review with the people who use them.
options.avoid: A plan with no budget or named owners.

options.name: An upkeep agreement
options.does: A written deal between the council, community groups, schools or vendors on who repaints, waters, prunes, refills and repairs.
options.keeps: Money from the running budget, not only the building budget.
options.avoid: Paying to build without paying to maintain.

cost.unit: year, for a cluster of assets

options.name: Map risk with the people exposed
options.does: Walk the area with workers, women, older and disabled people, migrants and renters to see who is exposed, why warnings fail, and where assets could go.
options.keeps: Repeating it as people and places change.
options.avoid: Relying on satellite heat maps alone.

options.name: A way to complain and be heard
options.does: An accessible route for complaints and feedback, set up before work starts.
options.keeps: Someone who answers within a set time.
options.avoid: Starting work where affected people have no voice or remedy.

options.name: Find the hooks in existing plans
options.does: Search city, disaster, water and climate plans and budgets for mandates and money that cooling can use.
options.keeps: Checking what you find with the officials concerned.
options.avoid: Assuming nothing exists because nobody uses the words “nature-based solutions”.

facts.fact: In Melbourne, officials found money for new green infrastructure was usually available, but running budgets were under pressure and rarely increased, even as the area to maintain grew.

source.label: Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023

facts.fact: In Santiago, without long-term financing, only better-off municipalities could take part in green-space programmes, because only they could afford the extra upkeep.

source.label: Hansen et al., chapter 10 in Nature-Based Solutions for Cities, 2023

facts.fact: Less than 10% of the climate finance that reaches cities goes to adaptation and resilience.

source.label: Cities Climate Finance Leadership Alliance, The State of Cities Climate Finance, 2021

facts.fact: The IUCN Global Standard for Nature-based Solutions makes inclusive governance and equity one of its eight criteria.

source.label: IUCN Global Standard: the eight criteria
